  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
  Negative Appraisals: Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Vignette:
Mai Nguyen, a 71-year-old lawyer who had spent decades building a reputation for calm precision in the courtroom, had not felt safe in her own body for eighteen months. The assault happened on a Tuesday evening after she’d stayed late to review a brief. In the dim underground garage of her office building, a man she had never seen before grabbed her from behind, clamped a hand over her mouth, and forced her against the concrete wall. He whispered obscenities close to her ear, his breath hot and damp, his eyes fixed on her with a knowing, degrading leer that she could still feel like a touch. She escaped by biting his hand and running, but what stayed with her was not only the violence—it was the sound of his breathing, the scrape of his shoes on the pavement, and the way her own heart had slammed so hard against her ribs that she thought it would tear through her chest.

In the months that followed, Mai’s world contracted. She had always been a woman who moved through the city with authority, but now every sudden sound—a car backfiring, a handbag zipper, the creak of a door—sent a bolt of alarm through her. What frightened her most, though, was the sensation of being looked at sexually. A passing glance from a stranger on the sidewalk, a client’s appreciative nod, even her husband’s affectionate gaze in the morning could trigger a wave of nausea and shame. She had come to believe that her own body had betrayed her: it had raced and trembled during the assault, and now it raced and trembled at the smallest things, proving she could no longer trust it. The world, she was certain, was a dangerous place, and the only way to survive was to remain on guard all the time.

That hypervigilance never relaxed. During the day, she could manage, but at night the threat felt physical—she checked locks three times, slept with the light on, and lay awake listening. When something took longer than expected, a delay at the pharmacy or a traffic jam on the way home, she immediately assumed something terrible was happening. Her fear was not abstract; it was a concrete expectation that danger was closing in. She began to avoid the parking garage altogether, and then any situation where she might be alone with a man. She stopped taking work home, refused to schedule meetings after four o’clock, and began asking her husband to drive her to the courthouse even though he had his own appointments. He did not complain, but she saw the worry in his face, and she hated that she could not explain why the rattle of the train or the sound of footsteps behind her on the street could leave her gasping for air.

The consequences extended into her work. Mai had always taken pride in arguing motions in open court, but now she found herself delegating oral arguments to junior associates. She told herself it was because she was tired, but the truth was that standing at the lectern, facing a gallery of faces, made her feel exposed—as if everyone could see what had happened to her. She began avoiding certain types of cases—any involving sexual harassment or assault—because the testimony would trigger her own memories, and she could not afford to lose composure. Her billable hours dropped. She started coming in late and leaving early. The partners noticed; she had to explain away her absences with vague references to health issues.

What finally brought her to seek help was an incident in the courthouse elevator. A colleague had complimented her suit, saying she looked “sharp,” and she had felt the old, familiar shame rise, then panic, then a full-blown attack in which she could not catch her breath. She excused herself, locked herself in a bathroom stall, and sobbed. That night, she told her husband she could not go on like this. She was afraid of the world, afraid of her own reactions, afraid that she had become someone she did not recognize. In the therapist’s office, she said she wanted to understand why she could not move past one Tuesday evening—why a sound, a glance, a racing heart could still undo her. She hoped, though she could barely say it aloud, that there might be a way to feel safe again, or at least to stop the constant watchfulness that had made her a stranger in her own life.
